splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines that carry criminal consequences.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's interpretation of ambiguous Guidelines provisions that expand criminal liability, or whether the rule of lenity should prevail. This matters because it determines whether ambiguous sentencing enhancements are construed in favor of the defendant or the government.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary controls over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines provisions, even in criminal sentencing contexts.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines commentary (Application Note 1) that expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy is entitled to deference under Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which adds conspiracy and other inchoate offenses to the career-offender definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid and authoritative interpretation of the guideline text. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders under the Sentencing Guidelines.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline and is entitled to deference under Stinson, even after Kisor, because the guideline text is genuinely ambiguous.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, so Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' and is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether a defendant must meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any one criterion is disqualifying. This split leads to dramatically different sentences for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on the circuit in which they are prosecuted.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in the provision.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule criminalizes a substance not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance at issue to be federally scheduled, or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies regardless of whether the substance is federally controlled. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines broadly includes any state-law drug offense, even if the substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

positions.label: Substance must be federally scheduled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in law, such as the First Step Act's amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) eliminating stacked mandatory minimums, can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can be considered — alone or in combination with other factors — as extraordinary and compelling reasons warranting sentence reduction through compassionate release. This split directly affects thousands of federal prisoners serving long stacked sentences under the pre-First Step Act § 924(c) regime.

positions.label: Non-retroactive change cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive change can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of (or as the sole basis for) a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, particularly in conjunction with the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement amendment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging a BOP decision about the conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring the challenge through a civil rights action (e.g., Bivens).
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists over whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging conditions and terms of confinement, or whether such challenges may also be brought as civil rights claims. This affects prisoners' ability to challenge BOP decisions on matters like First Step Act earned time credits and transfers to prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for challenges to confinement terms
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges the execution of a sentence, including BOP placement and credit decisions, habeas corpus is the sole federal remedy.

positions.label: Prisoners may use civil rights actions for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas and civil rights claims are not mutually exclusive; prisoners may bring non-habeas civil actions to challenge conditions and terms of confinement that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether appreciation in asset value that occurs after a Chapter 13 filing but before conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or the debtor. This matters significantly to debtors whose homes increase in value during the reorganization period, as it determines whether the trustee can sell the home to pay creditors.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), the broad scope of 'property of the estate' under § 541(a) means post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate, not the debtor, upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to debtors who convert in good faith, to protect the incentive to file under Chapter 13.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil deadline (30 days) or the criminal deadline (14 days) under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering a 30-day appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (triggering a 14-day deadline). This determines whether defendants' appeals of adverse fee rulings are timely.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline governs. This is the majority position.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is part of the criminal case, making the 14-day criminal appeal deadline applicable.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punishment for the violation of supervised release conditions when revoking supervised release, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether district courts may sentence defendants at supervised release revocation hearings based on the punitive purpose of punishing the violation itself, or only based on the breach of the court's trust. This affects the severity and rationale of revocation sentences imposed on hundreds of defendants annually.

positions.label: Courts may punish the underlying violation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose punishment for violations of supervised release conditions at revocation proceedings.

positions.label: Revocation sentences should focus on breach of trust
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release revocation sentences should be based on the defendant's breach of the court's trust, not punishment for the underlying violation conduct, consistent with the purpose of supervised release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate an employer's withdrawal liability from a multiemployer pension plan to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether the actuary may adopt assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be determined by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select or update actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current information in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund v. M & K Employee Solutions

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects sentencing outcomes for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Supervised release is tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the clock stops running and the court retains jurisdiction to revoke supervised release after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Supervised release is not tolled
positions.summary: Holds that courts lack authority to toll the term of supervised release absent explicit statutory authorization, so the supervisory term continues to run even when the supervisee absconds.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prohibits raising any claim previously presented — when bringing successive § 2255 motions, or whether they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s separate requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule. This affects the ability of federal prisoners to bring successive collateral attacks.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring any claim that was raised in a prior motion.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements for successive motions without the additional categorical bar.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the standards for evaluating whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting rules. The outcome affects whether election administration practices can be challenged before elections occur or must wait until after, with significant implications for mail-in voting and ballot-counting deadlines nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing for pre-election challenges
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when state laws allegedly dilute the value of lawful votes, allowing pre-election challenges to ballot-counting rules.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing absent concrete injury
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized competitive interest is insufficient for Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election without a showing of concrete, particularized injury.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Jacobson v. Florida Secretary of State

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits have not uniformly addressed whether denial of a motion to seal medical records qualifies as a collateral order immediately appealable under 28 U.S.C. § 1291. The D.C. Circuit held that medical privacy is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review, while other circuits have applied the collateral order doctrine more restrictively to sealing orders. This affects litigants' ability to protect sensitive health information during ongoing litigation.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that the denial of a motion to seal documents referencing private medical treatments and diagnoses is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be irreparably lost without immediate review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders generally are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because they can be adequately reviewed after final judgment.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Citizens First National Bank v. Cincinnati Insurance Co.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have applied differing standards to claims of discrimination in hospitality and business establishments, prompting SCOTUS review of the Second Circuit's approach. The decision could impact hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide by establishing or refining standards for fair treatment, discrimination liability, and damages.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Applies a broader standard for establishing liability for discrimination or unfair treatment in business establishments, making it easier for plaintiffs to prevail.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies a narrower standard requiring a higher showing for claims of discrimination in business operations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
